job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Hana Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at 7 and cycle to a regional energy company, where I'm a credit control assistant. I started in September after finishing my finance degree. I call customers who are behind on their gas bills and set up payment plans, and I log everything in the billing system. Some calls are lovely and some are heartbreaking. Evenings I'm in the flat I share with my friend Mara, studying for a professional exam and watching the heating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it was oversold. At work we'd keep using the billing system and the tools we already have. I'd tell Mara that some of the tools are handy, like drafting a reminder letter, but nobody is losing their job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm still not relaxed, because my contract is a one-year graduate contract and nobody has told me what happens after. I have about two weeks of savings and a student loan that arrives like a second landlord. Nothing about AI changes that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, make my probation count and ask my team lead, Ines, what the permanent roles look like. I'd keep using the AI writing helper for letters now and then, but I'd check every line. I'd also stay in the staff union, because I joined in my second week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, a little tense. It's the normal worry of being new and poor, not a big fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the one-year contract. What would you do if it wasn't renewed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Apply everywhere in the first week, including the water company and two banks. I have a good record on calls. Still, not many finance jobs near here pay enough to cover rent and the loan, so I'd probably have to move to the city and share a room again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why did you join the union so quickly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum is a hospital cleaner and she always said the union got her sick pay. When someone's overworked and nobody's looking, you want a group behind you. I know it's not glamorous.

say: The AI hype is **oversold**, and nobody at my firm is losing a job to it.
Some tools are handy for **reminder letters**, as long as I check them.
think: My one-year **graduate contract** has no promise of renewal.
I have **two weeks** of savings and a loan that feels like a second landlord.
do: Make **probation** count and ask my team lead Ines about permanent roles.
Stay in the **staff union** and check every AI-written letter line by line.
feel: Flat and a little **tense**, the ordinary worry of being new and poor.
S0.quote: my contract is a one-year graduate contract and nobody has told me what happens after
fieldNote: Her worry is the **contract**, not technology.
Uses AI sparingly and checks the output, which matches a steady adopter.
Mother's union experience shapes her instinct to **organise**.

steps.text: Ask team lead Ines what permanent credit control roles look like
Stay in the staff union and go to the spring meeting
Use the AI helper for reminder letters and check each line

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change the entry rungs first, and we should talk about it openly. Credit control has scripts and standard letters, which are exactly what software does well. The union should ask for a say before anything gets rolled out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my team of six could become a team of three who supervise a system. They already hired fewer people this year. Ines said they won't replace a woman leaving in spring. I'd be the newest, which means I'm first out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new system the minute it appears so I'm the person who understands it. I'd take the exam course on weekends, and ask to move to the hardship team, where the customers need a human voice. I'd cut my eating out entirely and put 80 a month aside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pressure in my chest, but I do have something I can do, and that helps. It's better than guessing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide when to learn the system and when to wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wait until I see colleagues I trust using it and it works. Then I'm in quickly. I'm not the first at anything, but I'm not the last either. I'd rather copy what works than be a guinea pig.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ines, who's 48 and has been there 22 years, and Gerda, who answers the phones and is about to be replaced by a chatbot. They don't have degrees. If they're cut, the firm saves money and nobody explains anything to them.

say: Entry rungs change first, so we must **talk openly** and give the union a say.
Credit control runs on **scripts and standard letters**, which software does well.
think: My team of six could shrink to **three**, and I'm the newest.
Ines (my team lead) won't replace a woman leaving in spring, which means **fewer hires**.
do: Learn the new system as soon as trusted colleagues show it works.
Take the exam course on weekends and ask to join the **hardship team**.
feel: **Pressure** in my chest, eased by having a plan.
S1.quote: I'm not the first at anything, but I'm not the last either. I'd rather copy what works than be a guinea pig.
fieldNote: Steady adopter: waits for **proof** from trusted colleagues, then moves fast.
Looks for the **human** part of the work as protection.
Worries about colleagues without degrees, which fits her progressive outlook.

steps.text: Learn the new billing system once colleagues I trust use it
Take the professional exam course on Saturday mornings
Put 80 a month into a savings account
Ask the union rep to raise software plans with management

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too fast for a society, and we need rules now. Governments should be thinking about income support and who owns the machines. I'd write to my local councillor, and I'd march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm terrified. A finance graduate with an average pass is the exact person a model replaces first. I'd have a year of experience, which is nothing. And the energy company would probably just hire software to chase bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay as long as they keep me, but I'd also start learning to do something that needs hands or a person's presence. Maybe a care-sector course or the electrician route. I'd cut back to bare rent, food and loan, and I'd ask Mara whether we can find a cheaper flat. I'd also go to every rally and sign up to anything about guaranteed income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, with a lump in my throat. A little angry, too, that it's being decided by a few companies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn something hands-on. Robots come about 3 years later in this picture. Does that change it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It buys me a little time, but not much. A trade is a bridge, not a place to stay. I'd rather my mum and I both have something to hold on to when the machines come for hands too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the loan is mine and she's not to worry. But I'd ask whether I could come home if I had to, and she'd say yes immediately and then lie awake. That's the part that makes me tear up.

say: Two years is too fast for a society, and we need **rules now**.
Governments should plan **income support** and ask who owns the machines.
think: A finance graduate with an average pass is the **first** a model replaces.
A year of experience is **nothing** to put on a job application.
do: Start a **care-sector** or electrician course for work that needs a person present.
Cut to bare **rent, food and loan**, and ask Mara about a cheaper flat.
feel: **Frightened**, with a lump in my throat, and angry that a few companies decide.
S2.quote: A finance graduate with an average pass is the exact person a model replaces first. I'd have a year of experience, which is nothing.
fieldNote: Expects to lose her role and has little cushion, so **alarmed**.
Considers a trade as a bridge, noting robots follow three years later.
Emotional peak is about her **mother** lying awake.

steps.text: Enrol on an evening care-sector or electrician course
Cut spending to rent, food and the loan payment
Write to my local councillor about income support
Join the rally and sign up to the guaranteed income campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd say we have just enough time if we act, and employers must fund retraining. I'd tell friends to learn a skill that stays human: care, teaching, negotiating with people in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd have two or three promotions' worth of time. By 27 I could be a supervisor in credit control, or in something else. But there's a good chance the pay band I'm aiming for disappears before I reach it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work the first year, keep the loan down, and finish my exam. Then I'd move to the hardship and welfare team, the one that sits with customers who can't pay. That's a job where a person is the point. I'd also learn the AI tools properly, since I'd be using them to prepare cases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steadier. A bit hopeful, if I'm honest, because five years is a fair amount of time to get my feet under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of you that likes this scenario?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. If I can be good at the human end of finance, I'd be needed. I like that thought. But it only works if I pay down the loan and have some savings, which is hard on my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money is tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Holidays, which I haven't had anyway, then the exam fees if the union can't help. I'd rather skip a new coat than fall behind on the loan.

say: We have **just enough time** if we act, and employers must fund retraining.
I'd tell friends to learn skills that stay **human**, like care and negotiating.
think: Five years could give me two or three **promotions** of time.
The pay band I'm aiming for might **vanish** before I reach it.
do: Work the first year, keep the loan down and finish the **exam**.
Move to the **hardship team** and learn the AI tools properly for case prep.
feel: **Steadier** and a bit hopeful, with time to get my feet under me.
S3.quote: If I can be good at the human end of finance, I'd be needed. I like that thought.
fieldNote: Plan is **human end of finance**, tied to a clear exam path.
Hope depends on debt and savings, so mood stays **anxious**.
Chooses unglamorous cuts: holidays, then exam fees.

steps.text: Pass the professional exam in June and ask for a pay review
Pay 60 a month extra off the student loan
Learn the AI case-preparation tools for the hardship team
Apply to move into the hardship and welfare team

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us the chance to build a fairer system, with a shorter week, public ownership of the biggest AI firms and strong unions. I'd get involved with a policy group now, while it's quiet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel okay about my own life. I'd be 32, with a loan cleared and maybe a mortgage conversation. But I'd be nervous that the world gets the warning and wastes it, like with the climate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay in finance, move around two or three employers for experience, and finish a master's part-time, maybe in public finance. I'd also start saving for a deposit. I'd use AI at work all the time by then because everyone would. And I'd keep paying union dues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite calm, actually. It's the one where I could imagine an ordinary life, a small flat and a cat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That nothing happens until the last two years, then a panic. People my age go on saying 'it's not here yet' and the politicians wait for headlines. I'd try to push things earlier, but I don't have any special power.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think you'd do differently from your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She never had a choice about the work. I'd have a profession and savings, so I could say no to a bad boss. I'd want to look after her better, maybe help with her rent, and I'd be proud of that.

say: Ten years lets us build a **fairer system**: shorter week, strong unions, public ownership.
I'd join a **policy group** now while things are quiet.
think: My own life looks fine: loan cleared and maybe a **mortgage** talk at 32.
I fear the world gets the warning and **wastes it**.
do: Move between two or three employers, and finish a **part-time master's** in public finance.
Save for a **deposit** and keep paying union dues.
feel: Quite **calm**, able to picture an ordinary life with a small flat.
S4.quote: I'd be nervous that the world gets the warning and wastes it, like with the climate.
fieldNote: Her worry shifts from her own job to **collective inertia**.
Wants to help her **mother** with rent, which gives the plan emotional stakes.
Mood is **uneasy** because own income looks safe but the world feels unready.

steps.text: Study a part-time master's in public finance
Save for a flat deposit by putting aside 150 a month
Join a local policy group on automation and work
Keep paying union dues and attend branch meetings

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd be one year into a career with no savings and a loan. What would help is income support that doesn't take months to arrive, and employers legally required to pay for retraining. And a rule that you can't replace a team without talking to the people in it. It would also help if my mum didn't have to carry my problems on top of her own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that I'm not against AI, and I use it myself. My concern is who gets the benefit. If we share it, great. If it's a few owners and the rest of us get a thank-you note, then we should be loud.

headlineQuote: I'm not against AI, and I use it myself. My concern is who gets the benefit. If we share it, great.
portrait: Hana is a **22-year-old** credit control assistant on a one-year graduate contract, living in a shared flat with Mara.
She has a heavy loan, about **two weeks** of savings and no family money to lean on.
She is progressive and union-minded, shaped by her mother's work as a hospital cleaner.
She adopts AI **once it's proven** and looks for the human end of finance as protection.
Her mood runs from tense in the slow case to **alarmed** with two years' warning, then eases with a decade.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when she would be a year into her career with no savings and a loan.
whatWouldHelp: **Fast income support**, employer-funded retraining, and a legal duty to consult staff before replacing teams.
